migrationNotes: Spine: a tile maker with a small square tile and an exact bigger copy. Cover the big tile with small ones to see the area grow by the factor times itself, turn that into a rule, use it on known areas and shrinking copies, then run it backwards with a square root.

lesson.title: When area scales

lead.text: To see how area changes, cover the big copy with copies of the small tile. Take a square tile and a larger copy whose sides are three times as long. Along one side of the big tile you can lay three small tiles. The big tile is also three small tiles tall, so there are three rows of them.

Counting gives 3 × 3 = 9 small tiles. The big tile has nine times the area of the small one, although its sides are only three times as long. The extra comes from the rows. A longer tile is also taller, and both changes add area.

afterFigure.text: The count follows the scale factor in both directions. With sides four times as long, four small tiles fit along an edge and there are four rows, so the big tile holds 4 × 4 = 16 small ones.

lead.text: Back at the tile shop. The small tile is 2 cm by 2 cm, and the large tile is a copy with sides twice as long.

Counting tiles works for squares, and other shapes need a rule. A rectangle's area is its width times its height. In a similar copy both of those lengths are multiplied by the scale factor, which we can call k. The new width is k times the old width, and the new height is k times the old height.

afterFigure.text: So the new area is (k × width) × (k × height), which equals k × k × (width × height). The old area has been multiplied by k × k, and that number is called the area factor. A rectangle 4 cm by 5 cm has an area of 20 cm². Scaling every length by 4 gives 16 cm by 20 cm. Its area is 320 cm², and 20 × 16 = 320 as the rule says.
The rule holds for any shape, as long as every length is multiplied by the same k. It breaks when only one length changes, because the second k is then missing.

lead.text: A square's area is its side times its side.

Often a problem gives an area and asks for the area of an enlargement, without any need for the sides. A logo might have an awkward outline that is hard to measure, but once its area is known the rule still works. Suppose a shape has area 8 cm² and a copy has every length tripled. The area factor is 3 × 3 = 9, so the copy has an area of 8 × 9 = 72 cm².

The rule also runs downwards. When the scale factor is less than 1, the copy is smaller and its area shrinks by the factor times itself. Halving every length gives an area factor of ½ × ½ = ¼. A shape of area 16 cm² has a half-size copy with area 4 cm², a quarter of the original.
Work out the area factor before you touch the area.

steps.headline: Going back to the length factor

lead.text: Sometimes the area factor is known and the length factor is the unknown. A map maker says that her new map has 49 times the area of the old one, and wants to know how much longer its lengths are. The area factor is the length factor times itself, so she needs the number that multiplies by itself to give 49.

That number is called the square root. The square root of 49 is 7, because 7 × 7 = 49, and so every length on the new map is 7 times as long. You can find a square root with the √ key on a calculator or by trying a few numbers. Squaring the answer gives you back the area factor, which is a check on your work.
A similar copy is described by its area, and the lengths are the unknown.
A designer stretches a banner in one direction only. Check which lengths actually change.

lesson.orientation: Distinguish a length scale factor from the resulting area factor.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A tile maker sells a small square tile, 2 cm on each side, and a larger tile that is an exact copy of it with every side twice as long. Both come in boxes that are priced by how much wall they cover.

The last lesson showed what happens to lengths in a copy: every one is multiplied by the scale factor. Covering a wall is not about lengths, though. It is about area, the amount of surface a tile covers, and a tile's area is made from two lengths, one across and one up. That raises a puzzle about what a scale factor does when it reaches both of them.

Printers, architects and people ordering paint all depend on the answer, because they need to know how much more paper, floor or paint a bigger copy takes. The lesson starts from the two tiles and builds the rule one step at a time.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find how area changes when every length is scaled, and go back from an area factor to a length factor.

recap.keyIdea: If every length is multiplied by k, the area is multiplied by k × k. Going back from an area factor to a length factor takes a square root.

blocks.text: A tile with sides twice as long holds 4 of the small tiles, and a shape of 6 cm² whose lengths are tripled covers 54 cm².
An area 9 times as big means the lengths are 3 times as long, and a banner stretched in one direction only has its area multiplied by 2.

recap.nextHook: Squares turn up in one more place. A walk of 3 m east and 4 m north has a shortcut across, and the next lesson shows how the squares of the two straight parts give the length of the shortcut.

questions.prompt: A 3 cm by 2 cm rectangle has both lengths doubled. Find the new area in square centimetres.
hints: Find the new width and the new height.
Multiply them to get the new area.
Work out 6 × 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The new rectangle is 6 by 4: 6 × 4 = 24 cm².

questions.onCorrect: 24 cm². Both lengths doubled, so the area is multiplied by 2 × 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That only doubles the area. Both the width and the height doubled.
That adds 4 to the area, but scaling multiplies lengths.

questions.prompt: A shape has area 6 cm². Every length is tripled in a similar copy. Find the new area in square centimetres.
hints: Area changes in two dimensions.
Square the length scale factor.
Calculate 6 × 3 × 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by 3 only. The factor works in two directions.
9 is the area factor. Multiply the area 6 by it.

questions.prompt: A shape has area 14 m². Every length is multiplied by 4 in a similar copy. Find the new area in square metres.
hints: Use the area factor, not just the length factor.
Multiply the original area by the square of four.
Calculate 14 × 4 × 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by 4 once. Area has two lengths, so use the factor twice.
16 is the area factor. Multiply the original area by it.

questions.prompt: A banner's width doubles while its height stays the same. By what number is its area multiplied?
hints: Track which dimensions change.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only one factor in width × height doubles, so the area doubles.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Only the width changes, so the area is multiplied only once by 2.

misconceptions.feedback: Squaring only applies when both lengths change. Here the height stays fixed.
8 is 2 × 2 × 2. Area has two lengths, and only one of them doubled.

questions.prompt: A similar copy has 9 times the area of the original. By what factor were the lengths multiplied?
hints: The area factor is the length factor times itself.
Going back from a squared number is a square root.
Try whole numbers multiplied by themselves until one of them reaches 9.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The positive factor whose square is 9 is 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Squaring undoes to square root: 3 × 3 = 9, so the lengths were tripled.

misconceptions.feedback: That squares 9. Go backwards: which number times itself gives the area factor?
That halves 9. Find the number that multiplies by itself to give it.

questions.prompt: A figure has area 20 cm². A similar copy halves every length. Find the copy's area in square centimetres.
hints: Halving both dimensions gives a quarter of the area.
Multiply the area by one-half twice.
Calculate 20/2/2.
questions.onCorrect: 5 cm². Halving every length multiplies the area by ½ × ½, which is a quarter.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves the area once. Both lengths halve, so halve twice.
That doubles the area. A smaller copy has less area.

questions.prompt: A square tile is 2 cm by 2 cm. A bigger copy has every side twice as long. How many of the small tiles would fit inside the big one?
hints: Picture the big tile covered in small tiles. How many fit along one side?
How many rows of that many are there?
Rows times tiles in a row.
questions.onCorrect: 4. Two small tiles fit along each side, and two rows of them: 2 × 2.

misconceptions.feedback: Two fit along one side, but the big tile also has two rows of them.
That counts three directions. A flat tile only has a length and a width.

questions.prompt: Every length of a square is multiplied by 5. By what number is its area multiplied?
hints: The length factor works on the width and on the height.
So it is used twice in the area.
Multiply 5 by 5.
questions.onCorrect: 25. The factor works on both lengths that make up the area: 5 × 5.

misconceptions.feedback: 5 is the length factor. Area uses two lengths, so the factor acts twice.
That adds 5 + 5. The factor multiplies, once in each direction.

questions.prompt: Why is the area multiplied by 3 × 3 and not just 3?
hints: How many lengths does area depend on?

acceptedIdeas: Area multiplies two lengths, and both are multiplied by 3.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Area multiplies two lengths, and both are multiplied by 3.

choices.label: Area multiplies two lengths, and both are multiplied by 3.

questions.onCorrect: Area is length × width. Multiply both by 3 and the area is multiplied by 3 × 3.

misconceptions.feedback: The size of the number doesn't matter. Count how many lengths the area depends on.
Only when every length is tripled. Another factor gives another area factor.

questions.prompt: A shape has area 3 m². A similar copy has every length multiplied by 10. What is the copy's area, in square metres?
hints: The area factor is the length factor used twice.
Work out 10 × 10.
Multiply the area by that.
questions.onCorrect: 300 m². The area factor is 10 × 10 = 100, and 3 × 100 = 300.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by 10 once. Area has two lengths, so use the factor twice.
100 is the area factor. Multiply the original area 3 by it.

questions.prompt: A similar copy has 16 times the area of the original. By what factor were the lengths multiplied?
hints: The area factor is the length factor times itself.
Which number times itself makes 16?
Try a few numbers multiplied by themselves.
questions.onCorrect: 4. The length factor squared is 16, and 4 × 4 = 16.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves 16. Find the number that multiplies by itself to give 16.
That squares 16. Go the other way: which number times itself gives 16?

citations.claim: Only one factor in width × height doubles, so the area doubles.
The positive factor whose square is 9 is 3.
25. The factor works on both lengths that make up the area: 5 × 5.
4. The length factor squared is 16, and 4 × 4 = 16.
A copy with sides k times as long holds k × k copies of the small tile.
A tile with sides twice as long holds 2 × 2 small tiles.
If every length is multiplied by k, the area is multiplied by k × k.
A square with each side multiplied by 5 has an area 25 times as big.
Multiply an area by the length factor squared, including factors below 1.
Tripling every length multiplies the area by 3 × 3 = 9.
The length factor is the square root of the area factor.
An area factor of 9 comes from a length factor of 3.
Doubling one length only multiplies the area by 2.
